paragraphs.heading: What counts as a gemstone
paragraphs.text: A gemstone is a piece of mineral crystal that is cut or polished and then used in jewelry or other adornments. Some rocks, such as lapis lazuli, opal and obsidian, are used for jewelry too and are often counted as gemstones. So, occasionally, are organic materials such as amber, jet and pearl, which are not minerals.

paragraphs.heading: Why hardness matters
paragraphs.text: Most gemstones are hard. Soft minerals are generally not used as gems, because they are brittle and do not last. There are exceptions: a softer mineral such as brazilianite may still be used in jewelry for its color, its luster or other physical properties that please the eye.

paragraphs.heading: Precious and semi-precious
paragraphs.text: In the West, the traditional way of sorting gems starts by dividing them into precious and semi-precious, and it goes back to the ancient Greeks. In modern use, four stones count as precious: emerald, ruby, sapphire and diamond. Every other gemstone is semi-precious. The split reflects how rare these stones were in ancient times and also their quality. All four are translucent and very hard, scoring 8 to 10 on the Mohs scale, and all but the colorless diamond show fine color in their purest forms.

paragraphs.heading: A label that can mislead
paragraphs.text: The traditional split does not always match what stones are worth now. Most garnets are fairly inexpensive, yet tsavorite, a green garnet, can be worth far more than an emerald of middling quality. The gemstone trade today no longer draws such a distinction. Even so, diamonds, rubies, sapphires and emeralds still have a reputation above that of other gemstones.

paragraphs.heading: Species and varieties
paragraphs.text: Gemstones are sorted into groups, species and varieties. Ruby, for example, is the red variety of the species corundum, and corundum of any other color is considered sapphire. Beryl has varieties too: emerald is green, aquamarine is blue, heliodor is yellow and morganite is pink.

paragraphs.heading: Grading by eye and by magnification
paragraphs.text: There is no grading system for gemstones that everyone accepts. Diamonds are graded with a system that the Gemological Institute of America (GIA) developed in the early 1950s. Historically, every gemstone was graded with the naked eye. The GIA system brought in 10x magnification as the standard for grading clarity. Other gemstones are still graded with the naked eye.

paragraphs.heading: The four Cs
paragraphs.text: The factors used to grade a diamond are summed up as the "four Cs": color, cut, clarity and carats. The four carry different weights for colored gemstones and for colorless diamonds. In diamonds, cut counts most toward value, followed by clarity and color. A diamond in its rough crystal form does not sparkle; it needs proper fashioning, and that is what "cut" means. In gemstones that have color, colored diamonds included, the purity and beauty of the color is the main thing that decides quality.
